newsitem.title: SYRIA: Israeli Arabs arrive in Syria to back peace stand.
newsitem.headline: Israeli Arabs arrive in Syria to back peace stand.

text.p: A group of Israeli Arabs arrived in Syria on Friday to discuss with President Hafez al-Assad the possibility of holding an Arab summit to put pressure on Israel to change its policy on peace in the Middle East.

The 44 delegates, including members of the opposition Meretz and Labour parties, flew in after a stopover in Cairo for an eight-day stay at the invitation of Assad. It is only the second such visit to Syria in 50 years.
Ibrahim Nemer Hussein, an independent Knesset member who heads the group, told reporters on arrival "We are not carrying any messages from Israel but love and peace for our brothers in Syria."
Hussein said the delegates want to show support for Syria's demand for the return of the Golan Heights, captured by Israel in the 1967 Arab-Israeli war.

Asked how the Arabs should react to the policies of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, he said "This is what I will discuss during my meeting with President Assad. What is required now is total Arab unity and a summit to unite Arab stands and powers to pressure Netanyahu."
"We highly estimate the Syrian stand and we see that Syria is ready for peace and that the ball is in the Israeli court now," he said.
"We want Israel to accept peace and the U.N. resolutions, to pull back to the 1967 borders... We want the Israeli government to accept facts and start with peace," Hussein said.
A similar group, including writers as well as politicians, came to Syria in 1994 to offer Assad condolences on his son Bassel's death.

Israel's previous Labour government, defeated by the right-wing Likud in 1996 elections, had favoured a land for peace deal and said an Israeli withdrawal from the Golan would match the depth of peace ties between the two countries.
But sporadic peace talks reached deadlock when Netanyahu rejected the idea of returning the Golan Heights in exchange for peace with Syria.

His recent support for a law that would require the backing of 80 of the 120 members of parliament for any territorial concessions, making it harder for Israel to give up the Golan Heights, soured relations between the two sides.
Raed Salah, head of the Islamic Movement and leader of a local council, told reporters it was important that the group show support for Syria's peace demands.
"It is necessary that we show our support for them. The Syrian stand gives the just and clear basis of the peace process, calling for Israel's withdrawal from the Golan," he said.

Israeli-Palestinian relations reached crisis point last week when Israel reacted to a suicide bomb attack in a Jerusalem market that killed 15 by sealing off the West Bank and Gaza Strip, stopping trade, freezing financial transfers and preventing Palestinians from going to work in Israel.

U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross is due in the region on Saturday on a mediation mission, but Hussein and Salah were pessimistic about his trip, saying it was not easy to influence the right-wing Israeli government.

"We wish that there could be any influence on the Israeli government, but we see that it is difficult... It is very difficult to imagine anyone influencing it, if change was not from inside (the government)," Hussein said.
"The American government has not shown up to now that it can put pressure on Israel," he added.
"I don't see that this visit (by Ross) carries any good news for the region," said Salah.
